tldr: A framework that takes a beautiful mesh produced by state-of-the-art 3D generative AI, decomposes it into watertight parts by material, assigns physical parameters like mass and hollow vs. solid geometry, and makes it instantly simulatable in physics engines.
hero_caption: A mesh created by 3D generative AI (TRELLIS) decomposed into material parts such as wood, ceramic, and plant by Gen2Physics, made watertight, density-estimated, and simulated in MuJoCo. Unlike prior methods (PUGS) that treat the entire object as a single mass, it reproduces natural behavior grounded in the physical properties of each part.
overview:
Generative AI capable of producing realistic 3D meshes from images in seconds is advancing rapidly, but attempting to load these outputs directly into a robotics simulator hits a major wall. Generated meshes are merely visually appealing "empty single skins." They contain no information about which parts are wood or metal, nor do they possess any physical parameters like mass or inertia tensors.

While existing studies estimate physical parameters using volumetric representations such as NeRF or 3D Gaussian Splatting, they cannot directly output meshes segmented into distinct parts, which robotics-standard rigid-body simulators like MuJoCo and Isaac Sim require. Furthermore, general 3D segmentation divides objects by semantic categories (e.g., "chair leg", "seat"), failing to capture material differences when a single leg combines both metal and rubber.

To solve this, the authors propose "Gen2Physics," a framework that takes any generated 3D mesh and performs dense material segmentation using multi-view rendering and a fine-tuned Vision Transformer (ViT). Cross-view prediction noise is geometrically reconciled through majority-voting projection onto mesh faces, and errors are further corrected using context reasoning via a large Vision-Language Model (VLM). Finally, each component is reconstructed into a complete, watertight mesh, and physical properties like mass are assigned while considering whether parts are solid or hollow.

In experiments, material identification accuracy (mIoU) jumped more than threefold from a baseline of 15.6% to 48.3%, while matching or exceeding prior mass-estimation accuracy on the real-world ABO-500 product dataset. This enables static generated meshes to be automatically converted into interactive simulation-ready assets for robots to manipulate.
contributions: Proposed a unified pipeline that automatically generates material-decomposed watertight sub-meshes ready for rigid-body physics simulation from a single mesh output by 3D generative models.
Developed a geometric consistency projection that robustly aggregates dense 2D ViT material segmentations into 3D via occlusion-aware majority voting across mesh faces.
Leveraged VLM contextual reasoning to correct material label failures and infer whether parts are solid or hollow, achieving more accurate volume and mass calculations.
Constructed PartNet-Material, a manually annotated benchmark dataset, and demonstrated more than double the material segmentation mIoU of prior methods.

sections.heading: Turning Beautiful 3D Meshes into Real Physics-Ready Simulation Assets
sections.summary: State-of-the-art 3D generative AI creates visually realistic meshes, but they lack physical properties and cannot run in robotics simulators. Gen2Physics solves this by automatically decomposing existing meshes by material and converting them into watertight parts compatible with physics engines.
sections.details:
With modern 3D generative models like TRELLIS and SPARC3D, remarkably high-fidelity textured meshes can be obtained from a single image. For robotics researchers, however, these are nothing more than "static decorative ornaments." Standard rigid-body and multi-body simulators like MuJoCo, NVIDIA Isaac Sim, and Bullet require objects not just as a single lumped mass, but as separate constituent parts, each assigned appropriate mass, center of mass, inertia tensor, and contact dynamics.

Prior studies based on NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have attempted to estimate physical properties, but because they operate on continuous density fields, they cannot directly output the discrete, part-separated meshes needed by rigid-body engines. In addition, recent 3D part segmentation models mostly segment by semantic categories such as "backrest" or "leg." Yet physical behavior is governed not by semantics, but by material. For instance, if only the tip of a chair leg is rubber while the rest is metal, their friction and mass characteristics differ completely.

To bridge this gap, this paper introduces Gen2Physics. It is generator-agnostic and functions as a post-processing framework for any arbitrary generated mesh. Based on the hypothesis that surface appearance and global context provide strong cues for physical properties, it applies dense material segmentation via a 2D Vision Transformer, integrates predictions into 3D consistently, and uses VLM reasoning to output simulation-ready watertight parts.

sections.heading: Why NeRF and Conventional Part Segmentation Fall Short
sections.summary: Recent physics-grounding approaches rely on volumetric representations like NeRF, which are incompatible with standard rigid-body physics engines. Existing 3D part segmentation also focuses on semantic categories rather than material boundaries, requiring a new approach that decomposes materials directly on meshes.
sections.details:
Related work falls broadly into three categories:

- **3D Generative Models and Part Reconstruction**: Technologies for generating high-quality meshes from text or images are progressing rapidly. In addition, methods such as HoloPart have emerged to reconstruct complete, closed sub-meshes from incomplete 3D patches, a technique leveraged in this pipeline.
- **3D Part Segmentation**: Methods directly segmenting 3D geometry (e.g., SAMPart3D, PartCrafter) are proliferating, but almost all target object instances or semantic parts. They cannot capture material boundaries vital for physical behavior, and many require specifying the number of target parts in advance. Combining generic segmenters like SAM also tends to align with geometric contours rather than material seams. Some work estimates materials in UV space, but this cannot be applied to generated meshes that lack clean UV parameterizations.
- **Physics Estimation from 3D Representations**: Frameworks like NeRF2Physics, PUGS, and PhysGen3D estimate density fields from volumetric representations such as NeRF, 3DGS, or voxels to run particle-based simulations (e.g., MPM). However, extracting clean, multi-material partitioned meshes from continuous density fields is exceptionally difficult. To integrate assets into rigid-body simulators standard in robotics, Gen2Physics's approach of directly isolating materials on meshes is essential.

sections.heading: Decomposing Meshes and Infusing Physics in Four Steps
sections.summary: The pipeline consists of four stages: (1) multi-view rendering and material segmentation with a ViT, (2) geometric consistency projection via per-face majority voting, (3) VLM-driven label refinement using contextual reasoning, and (4) part completion into watertight meshes with density and hollow structure estimation.
sections.details:
The Gen2Physics pipeline takes a generated mesh $M$ as input and produces a set of physically grounded, watertight components $\{P_1, P_2, \dots, P_k\}$.

- **3.1 Multi-View Material Segmentation**: First, the authors extracted 20,000 models from the Coohom interior asset collection, rendered them across multiple views in Unreal Engine, and automatically labeled them using a VLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash) to build a large-scale material dataset of 500,000 images. Material classes consist of 12 types adapted from PACO (wood, rubber, fabric, organic, leather, metal, paper, plastic, glass, ceramic, stone, and other). This data was used to fine-tune the DPT decoder of TIPS, a Vision Transformer with strong spatial feature extraction. At inference, the input mesh is rendered from 11 viewpoints, and material masks are predicted for each view.
- **3.2 2D-to-3D Geometric Consistency Projection**: Per-view predictions contain noise caused by lighting and occlusions. To resolve this, a face index buffer is rendered for each view to track visible mesh faces, and pixel-level predicted labels are cast as votes onto corresponding 3D mesh faces. The final face label $L_f$ is determined by a majority vote across all viewpoints. Unobserved occluded faces are assigned labels via flood filling from adjacent faces. This consistently groups disconnected components of the same material (such as four wooden legs) into the same class.
- **3.3 VLM-Guided Contextual Refinement**: Even with geometric consistency, optical reflections can cause semantic misidentifications. To correct this, the original RGB image, the color-coded 3D projected mask, and a material index table are passed to Gemini-2.5 Pro. Using a chain-of-thought prompt, the VLM performs context-based self-correction (e.g., reasoning that thin chair legs should be metal rather than wood).
- **3.4 Part Completion and Physical Grounding**: Grouping adjacent faces of the same material yields open surface patches (shells). These are passed into HoloPart for amodal completion into closed, watertight sub-meshes, hallucinating the unobserved backside. Next, the VLM infers a plausible density $\rho_i$ and whether each part's interior is solid or hollow. If hollow, it estimates wall thickness $t_i$. Mass is then calculated accurately as $m_i = \rho_i \cdot V_i$ for solid parts using volume $V_i$, and $m_i \approx \rho_i \cdot A_i \cdot t_i$ for hollow parts using surface area $A_i$.

captions.F2: The 2D-to-3D geometric consistency projection pipeline. While individual ViT view predictions contain noise, projecting and majority-voting onto mesh faces yields a coherent, artifact-free 3D material segmentation map.

sections.heading: More Than Double the Material Accuracy, Enabling Realistic Physics Simulation
sections.summary: On the PartNet-Material benchmark, Gen2Physics achieved an mIoU of 48.27%, vastly outperforming prior methods (~15%). It also matched state-of-the-art mass estimation on the ABO-500 benchmark while being the only approach to output simulation-ready watertight parts.
sections.details:
Evaluation was conducted along two axes: material identification accuracy and physical parameter (mass) estimation accuracy.

- **4.1–4.3 Material Segmentation Evaluation**: Using 100 PartNet models across 11 views, the authors constructed "PartNet-Material," a human-annotated validation set of 1,100 images, and compared Gen2Physics against NeRF2Physics and PUGS. To ensure fairness, identical mesh geometry, camera viewpoints, 12-class vocabulary, and VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) were used. While NeRF2Physics and PUGS achieved 14.54% and 15.56% mIoU respectively, Gen2Physics reached 48.27%—more than a threefold increase. Because baselines rely on local CLIP features, specular highlights fragment their masks. In contrast, fine-tuned ViT and VLM contextual reasoning extract smooth and accurate regions.
- **4.2 Mass Estimation Evaluation**: On the real-world ABO-500 dataset, Gen2Physics outperformed prior work in Minimum Ratio Error (MnRE), a metric robust to heavy-object bias, and matched the best baseline within 0.2% on Absolute Difference Error (ADE). While volumetric baselines rely on rigid uniform-thickness heuristics, Gen2Physics infers solid vs. hollow structure to compute volumes, yielding more physically plausible results.
- **4.4 Ablation Studies**: Removing VLM refinement ("ViT-only") caused mIoU to drop to 22.58%. Ceramic, in particular, scored 0.00% IoU with ViT alone due to confusion with plastic, but jumped to 43.49% once the VLM applied contextual reasoning. Furthermore, disabling internal structure inference and assuming all parts are solid artificially improved ADE due to dataset bias toward heavy items, but worsened relative error metrics (ALDE, APE, MnRE), validating the robustness of hollow-structure modeling.
- **4.5 Simulation Behavior Comparison**: In MuJoCo experiments, meshes from PUGS (which assign a lumped mass to the entire object) failed to exhibit realistic dynamics. In contrast, Gen2Physics assets, with accurate per-part density and centers of mass, produced intuitive and natural tipping and tumbling behaviors under external forces.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Work: How to Infer Unseen Internal Materials
sections.summary: Gen2Physics is a crucial step bridging the visual fidelity of 3D generative AI with the functional requirements of physics simulators. Key remaining challenges include dependence on an external completion model and estimating unseen internal materials.
sections.details:
This study establishes an automated pipeline to decompose generated 3D meshes by material and convert them into assets instantly usable in standard rigid-body simulators. However, several limitations remain before full practical deployment in robotics.

First, reconstructing watertight sub-meshes from surface patches currently relies on the external HoloPart model. Future work should explore an end-to-end architecture unifying segmentation and mesh completion. Second, the current pipeline primarily decomposes surface-visible materials. For composite assets with internal components like motors or batteries, mechanisms are needed to infer internal structures and heterogeneous fill ratios. Lastly, while the human-validated PartNet-Material dataset is precise, expanding beyond its current size of 1,100 images into a larger physical benchmark remains an important direction.

takeaways: Rigid-body physics simulation requires part decomposition based on material (density and friction) rather than semantic categories.
Projecting dense 2D ViT predictions onto 3D mesh faces via majority voting effectively suppresses cross-view noise.
Local texture misclassifications (e.g., confusing plastic with metal due to specular highlights) can be dramatically corrected by VLM object-level contextual reasoning.
Converting parts into watertight meshes and having a VLM infer solid vs. hollow structure enables realistic mass and inertia calculations without ad-hoc heuristics.
limitations: Relies on an external model (HoloPart) to complete surface patches into closed watertight sub-meshes, rather than operating end-to-end.
Focuses on surface-visible materials and cannot accurately estimate composite items with hidden, heavy internal components like electronics.
The manually validated PartNet-Material evaluation dataset is relatively modest in size at 1,100 images.
